How many of the above are considered "Distributed Energy Resources"?
x: All are correct: Distributed energy resources (DERs) are small-scale, decentralised energy resources in which electricity is generated near the point of use, often from renewable sources, rather than from centralised power plants. Examples of distributed energy resources (DERs) include rooftop solar photovoltaic units, battery storage systems, batteries in electric vehicles capable of exporting power back to the grid, combined heat and power (CHP) units, tri-generation systems that utilize waste heat for cooling, biomass generators fueled by waste gas or industrial and agricultural by-products, openand closedcycle gas turbines, reciprocating engines (diesel or oil-based), hydro and mini-hydro schemes, and fuel cells. These decentralised energy technologies can generate, store, or manage electricity close to the point of consumption, enhancing grid reliability and energy efficiency. PMF Concept Hack: Use simple understanding here — Distributed Energy Resources are small, decentralized energy systems located near the point of use rather than large centralized plants. Battery storage, biomass generators, fuel cells, and rooftop solar units all fit this idea. Since all four can generate/store energy locally, eliminating any option becomes difficult.

s: 'Net Metering' is sometimes seen in the news in the context of promoting :
o: the installation of CNG kits is motorcars
the installation of water meters in urban households
a billing mechanism for solar energy by consumers
the use of piped natural gas in the kitchens of
x: 'Net metering' is a billing mechanism that credits solar energy system owners for the electricity they add to the grid. For example, if a residential customer has a PV system on their roof, it may generate more electricity than the home uses during daylight hours. If the home is net-metered, the electricity meter will run backwards to provide a credit against what electricity is consumed at night or other periods when the home's electricity use exceeds the system's output. Customers are only billed for their 'net' energy use.
